summary:
West Sulawesi stands under Indonesia's national framework, and no province-specific finding for West Sulawesi was sourced, so the province is assessed against the national position. A visitor to West Sulawesi should expect the same legal and enforcement conditions that apply across Indonesia.

Consensual same-sex relations are effectively criminalised nationally. The penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment; because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, the provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Indonesia provides no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protections for LGBT people. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists "the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" among nonmilitary threats alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction, placing LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled.

Violence against trans people is documented and largely unpunished. In a wave of vigilante attacks on 14-16 July 2026, mobs attacked trans women across Indonesia, including over fifteen trans women doused, stripped and beaten in Bogor, with footage of the assaults shared online. Reporting from August 2026 ties that wave directly to the official securitisation of LGBTQ+ people. A separate raid on 22 June 2025 saw Indonesian police arrest 75 people, 74 men and one woman, from a privately rented villa in the Puncak area after public reports of a "gay party"; Amnesty International stated the gathering violated no law.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveller in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022 and died in custody; his mother alleges police beat him, while Indonesian police deny that violence was used.

Provincial religious and moral law forms part of the enforcement texture a visitor may encounter. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, homosexuality is punishable by flogging or imprisonment, and two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025; these punishments reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.

Legal gender recognition is restrictive: changing legal gender requires sex-reassignment surgery plus judicial approval, which affects the documents a trans visitor carries and presents at screening.
tangentialFactors:
No source surfaced a deviation from the national position in West Sulawesi large enough to score the province separately, so the province-specific record rests entirely on national material. Province-specific sources were not surfaced for West Sulawesi, and the dated national specifics ground the assessment.

Public attitudes have hardened. A researcher documented markedly hardened anti-queer attitudes since 2016, and a 2025 Pew Research figure put 93% of Indonesians calling homosexuality "morally unacceptable". Indonesia voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025.

Provincial moral laws and Aceh's caning regime remain the enforcement texture alongside the national penal code, and police have repeatedly raided private gay parties. The combination of a securitising presidential decree, hardened public attitudes and routine venue raids raises the risk of denunciation and mob action against a visibly trans visitor beyond what the formal text of the law alone would suggest.
localsOnly:
Residents of West Sulawesi live under the national penal code provision on extra-marital sex that took effect on 2 January 2026, and prosecutions under it are reported as selective rather than systematic.

Indonesian law offers residents no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and legal gender change for residents is conditional on sex-reassignment surgery plus judicial approval.

Residents face the same securitising official framing as visitors: the October 2025 presidential decree places "the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" among nonmilitary threats to be monitored and controlled. Private gatherings of LGBT people have been raided by police, and in Aceh residents have been publicly caned under provincial Sharia provisions.
outOfScopeNotes:
No province-specific source for West Sulawesi was located, so every claim in this record is national in origin and applied to the province by extension; whether West Sulawesi's own police or moral regulations diverge from the national pattern is unresolved and not sourced.

The sources disagree on the penalty for the extra-marital sex offence: the national framework entry gives up to two years' imprisonment, while one inventory source gives up to one year. The discrepancy is unresolved and not reconciled here.

Whether the October 2025 presidential decree has produced any operational directive, enforcement protocol or provincial implementation in West Sulawesi is not sourced. The frequency of venue raids or mob attacks specifically in West Sulawesi is likewise not sourced; the incidents cited occurred in other provinces and are used as evidence of the national pattern.
